Triage (finding first-touch): promoted to `pm:queue` — `domain:devx`, type Task. Direction ruled: **(2)** — give `declinedIn` the same two discriminators the recognizer got in #10793 (the narrow version: skip `typeDeclRegions`, the half `codeOnly` cannot cover and the half #10794's closure did not decide). Rationale: zero live instances today, but the failure mode is a loud false RED naming an accurate ledger's own type member — exactly the class the type-declaration exclusion exists to prevent — and (2) is the cheap change that closes it; (3) (folding into `declarationsIn`) stays available to the dev if it turns out equally cheap, since the file itself states that design goal twice. Dispatch condition carried from the card: the change moves the *declined* population, so it wants its own before/after against the `--bridge-coverage` header on the same terms #10683/#10793 did — expected measured delta today: **zero** (a nonzero delta is a stop-and-report, not a proceed).

Clause ② judged from content and not reached — this changes a CI gate's declined population, not the product's contract accept/reject behaviour.

All three symbols the card names (`declinedIn`, `declarationsIn`, `typeDeclRegions`, `bridgeCoverageFrom`) live in **`scripts/docs-audit/affected-docs.mjs`**, verified on `origin/main`. Note `bridgeCoverageFrom` is also referenced by `.github/workflows/docs-drift-check.yml`, so the `--bridge-coverage` header has a live consumer — check what that workflow does with it before changing the header's shape.

## Zone 1 — rulings (binding)

1. **The deliverable is that `declinedIn` stops deciding "in code position" for itself.** After #10793 it is the last scan in the file still doing so, and the file states the anti-drift goal twice in its own words: *"two scans that each decide separately what \"in code position\" means are two scans that can drift into disagreeing while both look right."*
2. **Route (2) or route (3) is YOUR call, made on measurement.** The card offers "give `declinedIn` the same two discriminators" (cheap, closes the class) and "fold it into `declarationsIn`" (bigger, removes the second opinion). Measure which is actually smaller in this file. ⛔ Do not pick (3) merely because it sounds more thorough, and do not pick (2) merely because it sounds safer.
3. ⛔ **Route (1) "leave it" is not available to you** — triage graded this `pm:queue`. If your measurement genuinely establishes that (1) is right, STOP and report with the evidence; do not close it on your own authority.
4. **A `--self-test` case is mandatory**, per this file's own rule and by the precedent of #10793 / #10683.
5. Scope: `scripts/docs-audit/affected-docs.mjs` and its self-test. ⛔ Do not touch the seven live ledgers, and ⛔ do not change #10722's rule about summing per-code tallies (different file, different card).

## Zone 2 — mechanism assumptions to falsify before you rely on them

- ⚠️ **The non-vacuity proof CANNOT come from the live tree, and this is the trap.** The card measures the live delta as **zero** — all seven ledgers declare `route: string;` and there are 0 quoted `route:`/`client:` leads inside any type declaration. So a green run proves nothing about your change. The failing-before/passing-after evidence has to come from a **synthetic fixture** (the card hands you one, in all three quote spellings), and the live before/after is a *safety* check whose predicted direction is NO CHANGE — state that prediction before running it.
- **Verify the claimed live-zero yourself rather than inheriting it.** It is a zero-hit reading across seven files and needs a positive control: show the same scan finds the leads when they ARE present (the fixture gives you that control for free).
- ⚠️ **`codeOnly` cannot reach this and never could** — the card is explicit that a type member is genuinely in code position, which is why #10794's closure does not settle it. If your reading suggests `codeOnly` is the answer, you have reproduced #10794 and should re-read.
- **The exclusion is load-bearing in the opposite direction.** The file's own `--self-test` note records that removing the type-declaration exclusion turns all seven accurate ledgers red (`259 of 266`). Whatever you do must not weaken that; measure it, don't assume your change is on the safe side of it.
- **Check whether the backtick spelling and the double-quote spelling take the same path.** The card measured both behaving identically, but it measured the *symptom*; do not assume one fix covers both without re-checking.

## Zone 3 — suggested routes (not binding)

- The card's reproduction (`parseLedgerSource` + `bridgeCoverageFrom` driven directly, with the two-member union) is a ready-made self-test fixture in all three quote spellings.
- #10793 is the direct precedent: it applied `typeDeclRegions` to the recognizer and to the first denominator term. Reading how it did that — and what before/after it presented — is likely cheaper than designing the evidence from scratch.
- If (3) turns out to be small, it is the outcome the file has been asking for twice over; say so with the measurement rather than with the adjective.

**ACCEPT** — PR **#11500**, head `c2fc7771`. (PR #11495 is closed and superseded; see below.)

The implementation was accepted in my earlier review. This confirms the re-landing and closes out the two rework rounds.

## Route (3) would have silently reversed a human's decision — verified

The strongest thing in this work is that route (3) was **built as a working probe and rejected on measurement**, not on adjective. It passes all 339 existing self-test cases, so a pass/fail signal could not have caught it; only a behavioural differential could. Two of the four populations it moves are uninvited, and one of them is #10794 — which I verified independently is `closed` / **`not_planned`, closed by a human** (`huangyiirene`, 2026-08-21). The thorough-looking route would have quietly undone a triage ruling, and nothing would have gone red.

## The re-landing, verified rather than accepted

| check | result |
|:---|:---|
| blob sha of `affected-docs.mjs` at old head `dc5d11b6` | `cac567a9bfb8c5691b3c914ed4b0acbbc5f7ca4d` |
| blob sha at new head `c2fc7771` | **identical** |
| closing-keyword scan of the new commit message | clean |
| **positive control** — same scan on the OLD message | **fires at line 26** |

That last row is what makes the third row mean anything: a grep that reports "clean" is worthless unless it is shown to still detect the thing it is looking for. It does.

## Two corrections you made to my instructions, both right

1. **My step-4 check was wrong.** `git diff <old-branch> <new-branch>` is not empty across different bases and should not be expected to be — it shows the intervening `main` commits. Your three-way check (identical blob, identical per-branch patch md5 with index lines stripped, identical `+184/-14`) is the one that discriminates. You also verified that nobody else touched the file between the two bases, so the whole-file checkout reverted no one — a risk I created with that instruction and did not name.
2. **`resolves` would not have fixed the original defect**, because `resolve/resolves/resolved` is itself a GitHub closing keyword. My proposed replacement was as broken as the string it replaced. You caught it instead of applying it.

You were also right to refuse the force-push and escalate. AGENTS.md multi-agent rule 3 is unconditional, and a PM seat cannot authorize a dev past a repo Prime Directive.

## Residual, and it is not yours

The superseded branch still exists at `dc5d11b6` with the keyword in its message. Deleting it failed **403 on both paths** — the REST ref endpoint and `git push --delete` — which is the proxy's write policy, not a repo permission. You verified that by **listing the ref** rather than trusting the delete's exit code, and reported it instead of routing around it, which is what the container's own README requires.

Escalated to the maintainer. The bounded risk: someone would have to reopen a closed, superseded PR and merge it, which would also re-apply a duplicate change — and the guard you added to the existing supersession comment names the consequence. A warning, not a control, and you said so.

## Out of scope

**#11494** filed: a `route:` whose value sits on the next line is counted twice in the denominator (`declinedIn` matches `\s*` after the colon, `declarationsIn` matches `[ \t]*`), byte-identical on `origin/main` and on this branch, zero live instances.

## CI

32 runs, **0 failure**, only `Lint & Repo Gates` outstanding — the gate that actually runs `check:docs-audit-scope` here, so landing waits for it. Verification will be by **content on `origin/main`**, with a positive control.

## What this card cost, and what it bought

Two rework rounds, neither about the code:

1. A closing keyword in the PR body — caught in review.
2. **The same keyword in the commit message**, which a pushed commit cannot shed without a force-push that AGENTS.md forbids unconditionally. That forced route D: a fresh branch, tree carried across by content, `#11495` closed as superseded. Proven byte-identical three ways before I accepted it, with the keyword scan shown to still fire on the old message so its silence on the new one meant something.

What it bought is worth more than that cost: route (3) — the option that looked more thorough, that the file's own docblock argues for twice, and that **passes all 339 existing self-test cases** — would have silently reversed #10794, a finding a human closed `not planned`. Only a behavioural differential could see that. It was found because the route was built and measured rather than reasoned about.

The residual is not yours: the superseded branch still carries `dc5d11b6` with the keyword, and deleting it failed 403 on both the REST ref endpoint and `git push --delete` — the proxy's write policy, not a repo permission. Escalated to the maintainer; the guard on #11495 names the consequence in the meantime.
